blocks.title: Medical and nutritional disclaimer
blocks.body: MamaBabyBites is an informational app designed for educational purposes only. The content, recipes, articles and suggestions in this app are not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Always seek the advice of your pediatrician, OB-GYN, family doctor or other qualified health provider with any questions about a medical condition, your baby's development or changes to your family's diet. Never ignore professional medical advice or delay seeking it because of something you read or tried in MamaBabyBites.

blocks.title: Feeding safety
blocks.body: This recipe is general inspiration, not a prescription. Every baby develops at their own pace. Always stay with your baby while they eat, test the temperature before serving, make sure the texture and size suit your baby's chewing and swallowing skills, and talk to your pediatrician before introducing major allergens.

blocks.title: Ages are a guide
blocks.body: Ages like 6, 7 or 9 months are general guidelines, not deadlines. Every baby gets there at their own pace. Before starting solids, look for signs of readiness, such as sitting up with little support and good head control, and talk to your pediatrician about your baby's needs.

blocks.title: Safety and allergen reminder
blocks.body: Serve foods in shapes, sizes and textures that suit your baby's age and chewing skills, such as thin slices, mashed or pureed, rather than whole round pieces. When offering a common allergen, watch your baby closely for signs of a reaction, and ask your pediatrician about timing and how often to offer it.

blocks.title: For general family meals
blocks.body: These recipes and articles are general meal inspiration. They aren't tailored to medical conditions, food allergies or special diets. Always check ingredient labels for allergens before serving.

blocks.title: Caring for you
blocks.body: Articles and self-care tips about postpartum recovery and well-being are for general information and support. They aren't therapy or medical treatment. If you have signs of postpartum depression or anxiety, or physical problems after birth, reach out to your doctor, midwife or a licensed mental health professional right away. In a crisis, call or text 988, or call 911.

blocks.title: Allergy safety
blocks.body: Food allergies can be severe and life-threatening. This article shares general US pediatric guidance for education; it doesn't replace medical advice or allergy testing. If your baby has severe eczema, a known food allergy or a family history of allergies, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist before offering major allergens. For signs of a severe reaction, like swelling of the lips or tongue, trouble breathing or hives all over, give epinephrine if it has been prescribed and call 911.

blocks.title: Emergency
blocks.body: If your baby is choking (silent, turning blue, can't breathe, cough or cry), call 911 right away and start back blows and chest thrusts.

blocks.title: Dental care note
blocks.body: This guide shares general tips based on pediatric dental guidance. For advice about your baby's teeth, fluoride or when to book the first dental visit, ask a pediatric dentist or your pediatrician.

blocks.title: Every child is different
blocks.body: Every child's relationship with food develops in its own way. These are supportive ideas, not clinical solutions. If your child strongly refuses food, is losing weight or has trouble swallowing, talk to your pediatrician or a pediatric feeding specialist.

blocks.title: About drinks
blocks.body: When to offer drinks like cow's milk and juice depends on your baby's age and development. Check with your pediatrician before offering cow's milk as a main drink or any juice, as every child's needs are different.

blocks.title: At your baby's own pace
blocks.body: Every baby builds chewing skills and iron stores at their own rate. If you're worried about your baby's iron, signs of anemia, or ongoing trouble chewing or swallowing, talk to your pediatrician or a pediatric feeding or speech therapist.

blocks.title: Where our guidance comes from
blocks.body: Our feeding timelines and safety tips are summarized from public health recommendations, mainly the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP and HealthyChildren.org), the CDC, the FDA and the USDA Dietary Guidelines, with the World Health Organization (WHO) for global context. Each article links to its sources. We share general information; we don't give individual medical advice.
